localChanges: In Civilization II games, barbarians raid from the sea and rise up near your cities, goody huts can release them, and a beaten leader pays a ransom. A New Game setting chooses how active they are, from Dormant to Fierce, or Random (#1008).

In Civilization II games, a destroyed computer civilization can come back as a new one, which a New Game setting can switch off, and a computer civilization that loses its capital can split in a civil war (#1008).
In Civilization II games, pollution warms the world: you're warned first, and then a warming turns coasts to swamp and jungle and dries out inland fields (#1008).
In Civilization II games, you can build a spaceship once anyone has built the Apollo Program and launch it once it can fly, and the first ship to land wins (#1008).
Once you have a spaceship, you can open it from the Game menu at any time (#1008).

Civilization II games have their own score and rating, which the score report explains in Civilization II's numbers and the game-over window and the Hall of Fame show, and the game-over window ranks you alongside one of 24 rulers of history (#1008).

Civilization II's Enhanced rules have three more, each off to start with: uprisings that gather around the city they threaten and tell you when they fail, barbarian cities that build the fighters of their age, and a score that charges each civilization only for its own pollution (#1008).

The search drew from a 13 × 13 box of storage coordinates, which on a staggered isometric grid is about 12 squares wide and 3 high, and on a hexagonal grid isn't a radius at all. It now draws from the topology's `area` within 6. The square grid draws as before, so Civ1 on it plays unchanged.

City#transfer(player) gives a city to another player as it is, for a civil war's rebels: no Captured rule runs, and the Transferred rules are told who has it now and who had it. Nothing calls it yet, so no game changes.

A Launchable rule says whether a ship may launch now, and launch() does nothing while one says no, so a ruleset can ask for a part on board first. With no Launchable rule, any ship launches as before.

The gate was the shape of the requirements, which Civilization II's parts will share once it registers them (the same six part classes, each needing an advance, and the Apollo Program at world range), so Civ1's policy would have played there before Civilization II has a policy of its own. It now plays only where the game's `LayoutRegistry` holds civ1-default-spaceship-layout's `Default` (or a layout made from it), which `createStrategies` takes from the game. The requirements are read each time, without a cache that a replaced entry would leave stale.

The scoring compared the signs of storage x and y, which on a staggered isometric grid aren't directions on the map. It now compares the logical axes there, and on the hexagonal grid, which has none, scores a step that brings the unit a move nearer the target +4 and one no further +2. The square grid scores as before.

`sail` took the first of each target's approaches as its path, which is undefined, not null, when a target has none; with no target reachable it then read `length` of undefined. The client caught the error and stood the ship down, so it now stands down without the error: play is unchanged. A ship with no city at all to sail for is still disbanded.

The Apollo Program and Space Flight, Plastics and Robotics come from the game's requirements, in the order the rule set lists them. Where they don't give every part this policy builds an advance and the parts an enabler (Civilization II's set today), the policy never plays for space: no Apollo, no space advances pushed. The final year stays Civ1's unless `createCiv1SpaceRacePolicy` is given another.

The leader and the polar exit come from base-barbarians' `LeadsGroup` and `LeavesMap` rules, with v474.05's answers (the group's Diplomat; 2 of 50 rows from either edge) while a rule set registers none, so Civ1 plays as before. A city's worth to a raider is base-barbarians' `cityGold`, the same formula in Civilization II. Irrigation and Mine come from their base packages, the same classes in both rule sets.

A rule set that hands every player a ship once anyone builds the Apollo Program, and makes its parts buildable (Civilization II's), got past the space race gate twice: `shouldLaunch` didn't ask it, so `LaunchSpaceship` would launch on Civ1's thresholds, and production's fallback ranked the parts with the improvements, ahead of Capitalization. `shouldLaunch` now answers no, and the fallback leaves the parts out, wherever `playsSpaceRace` (the gate: Civ1's layout and requirements) is false. On Civ1's layout nothing changes.
